quests.instruction: Your manager says, “Please turn off your phones.” Which spoken form fits the phrasal verb “turn off”?
options: “turn … off”, with a pause after the /n/
“tur-noff”, with the /n/ starting the particle
“tur-off”, with the /n/ left out so the vowels meet
quests.correctAnswer: “tur-noff”, with the /n/ starting the particle
quests.hint: Imagine the instruction given quickly before a meeting begins. Notice which sound of “turn” you can still hear when “off” starts.
quests.explanation: In “turn off”, the /n/ at the end of “turn” is followed by the vowel of “off”, so it is heard on the particle: “tur-noff”. Many everyday instructions are phrasal verbs, so hearing the verb and particle as one linked chunk speeds up your understanding.
quests.phoneticRule: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle that usually begins with a vowel, so the verb's final consonant commonly attaches to the particle.

quests.instruction: Why do phrasal verbs such as “pick up” so often sound like a single word?
options: Speakers treat every phrasal verb as one long word and skip the sounds at the boundary
The particle is stressed so strongly that it swallows the vowel of the verb
The particle begins with a vowel, so the verb’s final consonant attaches to it: “pi-kup”
quests.correctAnswer: The particle begins with a vowel, so the verb’s final consonant attaches to it: “pi-kup”
quests.hint: Say “pick up” slowly, then at normal speed. Compare where the /k/ sits each time.
quests.explanation: Verb + particle sequences are frequent, and the particles up, on, off, out and in all begin with vowels. That gives a ready-made link: the /k/ in “pick” joins “up”, so it sounds like “pi-kup”. Nothing is skipped; the boundary sounds simply sit in a new place.
quests.phoneticRule: The linking environment is created by the particle's initial vowel; the verb keeps all of its sounds, and only the syllable edge moves.

quests.instruction: Apply this to “sort out” in “We need to sort out the schedule.” Which chunking fits?
options: “sor-tout”, with the /t/ starting “out”
“sort … out”, with a stop of air after the /t/
“sor-out”, with the /t/ dropped so the vowels join
quests.correctAnswer: “sor-tout”, with the /t/ starting “out”
quests.hint: The verb ends in a /t/ and the particle starts with a vowel. Say it as part of the sentence and listen for the boundary.
quests.explanation: The /t/ that ends “sort” attaches to “out”: “sor-tout”. It is the same movement as in “turn off” and “pick up”, but with a /t/. When you meet a new phrasal verb, look for a final consonant followed by up, on, off, out or in.
quests.phoneticRule: The behaviour transfers to new phrasal verbs: identify the final consonant of the verb and the vowel-initial particle.

quests.instruction: Say “lots of it” at conversation speed. Which description matches what you hear?
options: Three separate words, each with its own clear start: “lots / of / it”
Only “of it” joins; “lots” stays apart because it ends in a plural /s/
“lot-su-vit”: the /s/ joins “of”, and the /v/ joins “it”
quests.correctAnswer: “lot-su-vit”: the /s/ joins “of”, and the /v/ joins “it”
quests.hint: Say it quickly and mark where each small word seems to begin.
quests.explanation: “Lots” ends in /s/ and “of” begins with a vowel, so the /s/ moves onto “of”. Then the /v/ of “of” moves onto “it”, giving “lot-su-vit”. The little word “of” is easy to lose, but it is held in place by the consonants on both sides.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak function words stay audible in fast speech partly because the consonants on either side attach to them, which creates a rhythmic chain.

quests.instruction: Choose the explanation that fits “lack of ideas” said fluently.
options: The word “of” is reduced so far that it is deleted, leaving only “lack ideas”
The /k/ links to “of”, but a small break after “of” lets “ideas” start with a clean vowel
The /k/ links to “of”, and the /v/ of “of” links to “ideas”: “la-ku-videas”
quests.correctAnswer: The /k/ links to “of”, and the /v/ of “of” links to “ideas”: “la-ku-videas”
quests.hint: Both “lack” and “of” end in consonants. Check what follows each one.
quests.explanation: “Lack” ends in /k/ and “of” starts with a vowel; “of” ends in /v/ and “ideas” starts with a vowel. So both consonants shift: “la-ku-videas”. The word “of” is tucked in the middle, which is why it can be hard to hear.
quests.phoneticRule: Because “of” starts with a vowel and ends with /v/, it acts as a bridge in a chain: it links back to a consonant-final word and forward to a vowel-initial one.

quests.instruction: You see the sign “out of order” on a lift. Which spoken form fits the phrase?
options: “out … of … order”, with each word separated by a small stop
“ou-tu-vorder”, with the /t/ joining “of” and the /v/ joining “order”
“ou-tu-order”, with the /v/ omitted
quests.correctAnswer: “ou-tu-vorder”, with the /t/ joining “of” and the /v/ joining “order”
quests.hint: Picture the sign on a broken machine. Say it fast and notice which small word sits between two links.
quests.explanation: “Out” ends in /t/ and “of” begins with a vowel, so the /t/ moves onto “of”. The /v/ from “of” then moves onto “order”. You hear “ou-tu-vorder”. Signs and notices are read quickly, so spotting the chain helps.
quests.phoneticRule: The bridging behaviour of “of” appears in fixed phrases, where the preposition passes its /v/ to a following vowel-initial noun.

quests.instruction: It is stuffy in a meeting room and someone offers, “Shall I open the window?” Which spoken form fits the start of the offer?
options: “sha-lai open”, with the /l/ joined to “I”
“shall … I open”, with a break after “shall”
“sha-lopen”, with “I” disappearing between the words
quests.correctAnswer: “sha-lai open”, with the /l/ joined to “I”
quests.hint: Imagine offering quickly, without wanting to interrupt. Listen for what the first word’s last sound does when the pronoun follows.
quests.explanation: “Shall” ends in /l/ and “I” starts with a vowel sound, so the /l/ attaches to “I”: “sha-lai”. Offers are usually short and quick, so this small shift is part of how they flow. The pronoun is still there; it simply sounds attached to “shall”.
quests.phoneticRule: In offers and requests, a subject pronoun beginning with a vowel commonly receives the final consonant of the preceding modal verb.

quests.instruction: Someone asks, “Can I use a pen?” Why does “use a” sound like “yoo-za”?
options: The last letter of “use” is silent, so the /j/ at the start moves to “a”
“Use” ends in the sound /z/, not /s/, and that /z/ attaches to “a”
A /z/ is added because “a” needs a consonant before it
quests.correctAnswer: “Use” ends in the sound /z/, not /s/, and that /z/ attaches to “a”
quests.hint: Say the verb “use” on its own and listen to its last sound, then decide what follows it.
quests.explanation: In the verb “use”, the final sound is /z/. When “a” follows, the /z/ attaches to it: “yoo-za pen”. Spelling with an “s” can hide a /z/ sound; linking follows the sound, not the letter.
quests.phoneticRule: The consonant that links is the one actually pronounced at the end of the word, which may differ from the spelled letter (for example /z/ for “s” in the verb “use”).

quests.instruction: You phone a clinic to book a visit. Which spoken form fits “make an appointment”?
options: “make … an … appointment”, with a small break before each vowel-initial word
“may-ka-appointment”, with the /n/ of “an” left out before the noun
“may-ka-nappointment”, with /k/ and /n/ each starting the next syllable
quests.correctAnswer: “may-ka-nappointment”, with /k/ and /n/ each starting the next syllable
quests.hint: Say the request as if you are on the phone. Find the two places where a consonant meets a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Make” ends in /k/ and “an” starts with a vowel, so the /k/ joins “an”. Then the /n/ of “an” joins “appointment”: “may-ka-nappointment”. Booking phrases often contain several small words, so chains like this are common.
quests.phoneticRule: In requests, an article ending in /n/ passes its consonant on to a vowel-initial noun, so “an + noun” chunks are often heard as a single shape.

quests.instruction: Predict which consonants change position in “in an office”.
options: Both /n/ sounds: the first joins “an” and the second joins “office”
Only the /n/ of “in”, because “an” is too weak to pass on a consonant
The /n/ of “an” and the /s/ of “office”
quests.correctAnswer: Both /n/ sounds: the first joins “an” and the second joins “office”
quests.hint: Write the three words, circle each word-final consonant, and check what follows it.
quests.explanation: “In” ends in /n/ and “an” begins with a vowel, so the first /n/ joins “an”. “An” also ends in /n/ and “office” begins with a vowel, so the second /n/ joins “office”: “i-na-noffice”. The last sound of “office” has nothing after it in this chunk.
quests.phoneticRule: A weak article can pass a consonant on: it receives the previous word's final consonant and, if it also ends in one, hands that one to the next vowel-initial word.

quests.instruction: Choose the explanation that fits “stand in a line” in a queue announcement.
options: The /d/ of “stand” joins “in”, and the /n/ of “in” joins “a”: “stan-di-na line”
Only “stand in” links; “in a” has a clear break because “a” is very short
The /d/ is dropped, so “stan” and “in” blend into “stanin” before “a line”
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ of “stand” joins “in”, and the /n/ of “in” joins “a”: “stan-di-na line”
quests.hint: Say it as a call from a person managing a queue, and mark each consonant that begins the next beat.
quests.explanation: “Stand” ends in /d/, which joins “in”. “In” ends in /n/, which joins “a”. That gives “stan-di-na line”. The small words carry the links, so listen for the small words as well as the nouns.
quests.phoneticRule: Consecutive links can be carried entirely by function words, so the content words at the edges are often the easiest part of the chunk to hear.

quests.instruction: Apply the idea to “write it up” in “I’ll write it up tonight.” Which spoken form fits?
options: “rai-tit up”, with only the first link happening and the second /t/ staying on “it”
“write … it … up”, each word closed off with its own clear stop before the next
“rai-ti-tup”, with the /t/ of “write” joining “it” and the /t/ of “it” joining “up”
quests.correctAnswer: “rai-ti-tup”, with the /t/ of “write” joining “it” and the /t/ of “it” joining “up”
quests.hint: Both /t/ sounds are followed by vowels. Say it fast and check where each one lands.
quests.explanation: The first /t/ (from “write”) attaches to “it”, and the second /t/ (from “it”) attaches to “up”: “rai-ti-tup”. It is a common phrase in work talk. Predicting the same shape as in earlier chains helps you recognise it at once.
quests.phoneticRule: Repeated consonants across neighbouring links, such as two /t/ sounds, are each tied to their own following vowel rather than merged.

quests.instruction: In “Wait, I’ll check”, the speaker pauses briefly after “wait”. What does the pause do to the /t/?
options: It makes the /t/ stronger, so it moves even more firmly onto “I’ll”
It keeps the /t/ with “wait”, so it does not move onto “I’ll”
It removes the /t/ completely because the words are far apart
quests.correctAnswer: It keeps the /t/ with “wait”, so it does not move onto “I’ll”
quests.hint: Think about what a comma or a pause does to the flow of sound. Does the /t/ have a vowel right after it?
quests.explanation: Linking works most clearly inside a phrase, where the sounds run on without a break. When a speaker pauses after “wait”, the /t/ stays with that word and “I’ll” begins a new chunk. Learners who link across every pause can sound rushed.
quests.phoneticRule: Consonant-to-vowel linking normally operates within a phrase or thought group; a clear pause usually blocks it, although listeners may still hear a short release of the consonant.

quests.instruction: A speaker says “That’s enough I think” as one phrase, with no pause after “enough”. What happens at that boundary?
options: The /f/ links to “I”: “enou-fai think”
The /f/ is dropped, because “I” starts a separate thought
The /f/ becomes a /v/ before the pronoun
quests.correctAnswer: The /f/ links to “I”: “enou-fai think”
quests.hint: Say the sentence as one continuous phrase, with no stop after “enough”. Listen for what follows the /f/.
quests.explanation: With no pause, “enough” and “I” belong to the same phrase, so the /f/ attaches to “I”: “enou-fai think”. Compare this with “Wait, I’ll check”, where a pause keeps the words apart. Phrase grouping decides whether a link is available.
quests.phoneticRule: Phrase grouping controls linking: the same word pair can link when spoken as one phrase and stay separate when a pause or clear phrase boundary intervenes.

quests.instruction: Which statement fits the boundaries in “Come at eight, I’ll be there”?
quests.word: Come at eight, I’ll be there
quests.textToSpeak: Come at eight, I’ll be there
options: Both boundaries link, because commas are ignored when people speak quickly and casually
“Come at” links (“cuh-mat”), but the pause after “eight” keeps the /t/ from joining “I’ll”
Neither boundary links, because “at” and “I’ll” are both too short to receive a consonant
quests.correctAnswer: “Come at” links (“cuh-mat”), but the pause after “eight” keeps the /t/ from joining “I’ll”
quests.hint: Look at the punctuation: one boundary is inside a phrase and one is not. Which one gives a consonant the chance to move?
quests.explanation: “Come” ends in /m/ and “at” starts with a vowel, and there is no pause between them, so you hear “cuh-mat”. After “eight” the speaker pauses, so the /t/ stays on “eight” and “I’ll” starts a fresh chunk. Reading punctuation as a hint to phrasing helps you predict where links will not happen.
quests.phoneticRule: Punctuation often reflects phrasing: a comma-type boundary is a likely place for a pause and therefore for the absence of a link.

quests.instruction: It is nearly the end of the working day and someone says “five o’clock”. Choose the most natural spoken form.
options: “five … uh-clock”, with a short stop before the vowel
“fai-uh-clock”, with the /v/ left out
“fai-vuh-clock”, with the /v/ starting the next syllable
quests.correctAnswer: “fai-vuh-clock”, with the /v/ starting the next syllable
quests.hint: Say the time the way you would when checking your watch: quickly and lightly. Notice the last sound of “five”.
quests.explanation: “Five” ends in /v/, and “o’clock” begins with a weak vowel, so the /v/ moves across: “fai-vuh-clock”. Times of day are short and repeated, which makes them a good place to practise hearing links.
quests.phoneticRule: Numbers ending in a consonant link to a following vowel-initial word such as “o’clock”, which is why times are heard as one unit.

quests.instruction: In “thirteen or fourteen”, which sound moves to the start of “or”?
options: The /t/ from the middle of “thirteen”
The /n/ ending “thirteen”
The /f/ from the start of “fourteen”
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/ ending “thirteen”
quests.hint: Say the two numbers as if giving a rough estimate. Listen for what the word “or” seems to begin with.
quests.explanation: “Thirteen” ends in /n/, and “or” begins with a vowel, so the /n/ is heard on “or”: “thur-tee-nor four-teen”. The stressed vowel stays where it is, so only the final consonant moves. Estimates like this are common in everyday number talk.
quests.phoneticRule: Number words behave like ordinary words for linking: a final /n/ can attach to a following vowel even when the number ends in a stressed syllable.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “around eleven” in “Let’s meet around eleven.” Which spoken form fits?
options: “a-round … eleven”, with a clear stop after the /d/ before the vowel
“a-roun-di-leven”, with the /d/ starting the vowel of “eleven”
“a-roun-ne-leven”, with the /d/ changing into an /n/ before “eleven”
quests.correctAnswer: “a-roun-di-leven”, with the /d/ starting the vowel of “eleven”
quests.hint: Look at the last sound of “around” and the first sound of “eleven”. Say the phrase without stopping.
quests.explanation: “Around” ends in /d/ and “eleven” begins with a vowel, so the /d/ attaches to it: “a-roun-di-leven”. Time expressions with vowel-initial numbers are common in plans, so noticing the link helps you catch the hour.
quests.phoneticRule: Time expressions with vowel-initial numbers such as “eleven” receive the final consonant of a preceding word, so the number seems to begin with that consonant.

quests.instruction: Say “Sam and I” as it would sound at the start of “Sam and I are late.” Which description fits?
options: Both links happen: the /m/ joins “and”, and the /d/ often joins “I”
Only the /d/ joins “I”; “Sam” stays separate
“And” is dropped, leaving “Sam” and “I” to connect directly
quests.correctAnswer: Both links happen: the /m/ joins “and”, and the /d/ often joins “I”
quests.hint: Say the phrase as part of the sentence. Count the beats and note what starts each one.
quests.explanation: “Sam” ends in /m/ and “and” begins with a vowel, so the /m/ attaches to “and”. “And” ends in /d/ and “I” is a vowel, so the /d/ often attaches to “I”. The result is a compact “sa-man-dai” at the start of a clause. Conjunctions link like any other word.
quests.phoneticRule: Conjunctions that begin with vowels, such as “and”, take on the final consonant of the preceding word and can pass on their own consonant to a following vowel.

quests.instruction: At the start of a clause, “but if it rains” seems to lose its word edges. What explains this?
options: The conjunction “but” is stressed so strongly that it swallows the start of the next word
A pause before “if” stops the /t/ from moving, so the words stay separate and clear
Each word ends in a consonant and the next begins with a vowel, so /t/ and /f/ each start a beat
quests.correctAnswer: Each word ends in a consonant and the next begins with a vowel, so /t/ and /f/ each start a beat
quests.hint: Look at how many consonant-to-vowel boundaries there are in the first three words, then say them without stopping.
quests.explanation: “But” ends in /t/ and “if” begins with a vowel, so you hear “bu-tif”. “If” ends in /f/ and “it” begins with a vowel, so you hear “i-fit”. Together they form “bu-ti-fit”, a shape that turns up at the start of many conditions. Knowing it helps you catch the start of the clause before the main idea arrives.
quests.phoneticRule: Clause-initial conjunctions and small pronouns form links like any other words, so conditional openings are often heard as one fast chunk.

quests.instruction: Someone reminds you of something they said earlier: “as I said”. Which spoken form fits?
options: “uh-zai said”, with the /z/ joined to “I”
“as … I said”, with a pause after “as”
“uh-sai said”, with the /z/ turning into an /s/
quests.correctAnswer: “uh-zai said”, with the /z/ joined to “I”
quests.hint: Think of how a speaker would say it while returning to an earlier point. What does the buzzing sound of “as” attach to?
quests.explanation: “As” ends in /z/, and “I” begins with a vowel, so the /z/ moves onto “I”: “uh-zai said”. The buzz stays voiced, so it does not turn into /s/. Clause openers such as “as I said” are short and quick, so noticing the link helps you follow the sentence.
quests.phoneticRule: A voiced final consonant remains voiced when it links into a following pronoun, including at the start of a clause.

quests.instruction: Identify why “time ago” links even though “time” is spelled with a final “e”.
options: The final “e” is pronounced, so it forms a vowel that joins “ago”
Words ending in the letter “e” cannot link, because they look as if they end in a vowel
The letter “e” is silent, so “time” ends in /m/, and the /m/ attaches to “ago”
quests.correctAnswer: The letter “e” is silent, so “time” ends in /m/, and the /m/ attaches to “ago”
quests.hint: Say “time” on its own and identify its last sound, ignoring the spelling.
quests.explanation: Spelling suggests that “time” ends in a vowel, but the final “e” is silent and the word ends in /m/. So the /m/ is free to link to “ago”: “tai-ma-go”. Judging by sound, not spelling, is the reliable way to predict links.
quests.phoneticRule: The link is decided by the final sound of the word, not the final letter, so words with a silent final “e” behave like consonant-final words.

quests.instruction: Compare “make it” with “see it”. Why does only “make it” have a consonant link?
options: “See” contains a silent letter, so no sound is left over to move onto “it”
“Make” ends in the consonant /k/ despite its spelled “e”, while “see” ends in a vowel
“Make” is a longer word, so it has more sounds available to move onto “it”
quests.correctAnswer: “Make” ends in the consonant /k/ despite its spelled “e”, while “see” ends in a vowel
quests.hint: Ignore the spelling and say each first word alone. What is the very last sound you make?
quests.explanation: “Make” ends with the sound /k/, so it can attach to “it” and give “may-kit”. “See” ends with the vowel /iː/, so no consonant is available to move; a different kind of link happens there, which you will meet soon. The silent “e” in “make” does not count as a sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Consonant-to-vowel linking depends on whether the last sound of a word is a consonant; a silent final letter does not create a vowel ending.

quests.instruction: On a crowded bench you hear “Could you move over?” Which spoken form fits “move over”?
options: “moo-vover”, with the /v/ starting “over”
“moo-over”, with the /v/ dropped because the letter “e” is silent
“move … over”, with a stop after the /v/
quests.correctAnswer: “moo-vover”, with the /v/ starting “over”
quests.hint: The word “move” ends with a silent letter. Which sound do you actually finish on?
quests.explanation: “Move” ends with /v/ despite the silent “e”, and “over” begins with a vowel, so the /v/ attaches to it: “moo-vover”. It is a useful chunk in shared spaces such as buses and benches. As with “time ago”, the sound, not the spelling, tells you where the link is.
quests.phoneticRule: Words with a silent final “e” (such as “move”, “time” and “make”) end in a consonant sound, so they link to a following vowel just like words ending in a consonant letter.

quests.instruction: At a ticket office you hear “Sorry, sold out.” Which spoken form fits “sold out”?
options: “sold … out”, with the /d/ closed off before a stop
“sol-dout”, with the /d/ starting “out”
“sol-out”, with the /d/ dropped between the two words
quests.correctAnswer: “sol-dout”, with the /d/ starting “out”
quests.hint: Imagine the person behind the counter saying it in a hurry. Listen for which sound of “sold” is still with that word when “out” begins.
quests.explanation: “Sold” ends in the cluster /ld/. The /d/ attaches to “out”, giving “sol-dout”, while the /l/ stays with “sold”. Shop and travel notices are said quickly, so recognising the shape helps you understand them.
quests.phoneticRule: Consonant clusters such as /ld/ release only the last consonant to the next vowel, so “sold out” is heard with the /d/ starting “out”.

quests.instruction: At a till the assistant asks, “Cash or card?” Which sound from “cash” is heard at the start of “or”?
options: /ʃ/ (the “sh” sound), the last sound of “cash”
/k/, the first sound of “cash”
/d/, the last sound of “card”
quests.correctAnswer: /ʃ/ (the “sh” sound), the last sound of “cash”
quests.hint: Think of a shop assistant asking the question quickly. Listen for what begins the word “or”.
quests.explanation: “Cash” ends in the sound /ʃ/, spelled “sh”, and “or” begins with a vowel, so the /ʃ/ attaches to it: “ca-shor card”. The question is very common at a till, and the link makes “or” easy to overlook.
quests.phoneticRule: The weak conjunction “or” begins with a vowel and readily receives the final consonant of the preceding word.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “get off” in “Where should I get off?” Which spoken form fits?
options: “get … off”, with a stop after the /t/
“ge-off”, with the /t/ dropped so the vowels join
“ge-toff”, with the /t/ starting “off”
quests.correctAnswer: “ge-toff”, with the /t/ starting “off”
quests.hint: Imagine asking a bus driver. Notice what the /t/ does when “off” follows straight away.
quests.explanation: “Get” ends in /t/ and “off” begins with a vowel, so the /t/ attaches to it: “ge-toff”. In some accents the /t/ may be a brief throat stop or a quick tap, but it still belongs with “off”. Travel questions are short, so spotting the link helps you hear them.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /t/ can be realised in different ways depending on accent, but before a vowel-initial word it commonly attaches to that word.

quests.instruction: Which boundaries in “put a coat on” are linked by a consonant followed by a vowel?
options: “put a” and “a coat”
“a coat” and “coat on”
“put a” and “coat on”
quests.correctAnswer: “put a” and “coat on”
quests.hint: Say the phrase slowly, then check each of the three boundaries for a consonant followed by a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Put” ends in /t/ and “a” is a vowel, so they link (“pu-ta”). “Coat” ends in /t/ and “on” begins with a vowel, so they link too (“coa-ton”). “A coat” is vowel + consonant, so it does not link. The natural rhythm is “pu-ta coa-ton”.
quests.phoneticRule: In a four-word phrase, three boundaries are checked in turn; only those with a consonant sound followed by a vowel sound show consonant-to-vowel linking.

quests.instruction: In a waiting room someone says, “Sit on a chair.” Which version matches fluent speech?
options: “si-to-na chair”, with links after “sit” and after “on”
“si-ton a chair”, with only the first link
“sit … on … a chair”, with no links at all
quests.correctAnswer: “si-to-na chair”, with links after “sit” and after “on”
quests.hint: Find every boundary where a consonant meets a vowel, and check what sound “chair” starts with.
quests.explanation: Two boundaries qualify: /t/ + “on” and /n/ + “a”. You therefore hear “si-to-na chair”. There is no link before “chair” because “a” ends in a vowel and “chair” begins with a consonant. Practise reading four-word phrases boundary by boundary.
quests.phoneticRule: The last boundary must be judged like the others: when a vowel is followed by a consonant-initial word, there is no consonant-to-vowel link.

quests.instruction: Apply everything from this level to “hand in an essay”. Which spoken form fits?
options: “han-di-nan essay”, with only the first two links
“han-di-na-nessay”, with a link at each of the three boundaries
“hand … in … an … essay”, with a stop before each vowel-initial word
quests.correctAnswer: “han-di-na-nessay”, with a link at each of the three boundaries
quests.hint: Every boundary in this phrase has a consonant on the left and a vowel on the right. Count them before you choose.
quests.explanation: “Hand” ends in /d/, “in” ends in /n/, and “an” ends in /n/; each is followed by a vowel-initial word. So all three consonants move forward: “han-di-na-nessay”. It looks like a lot, but the rule is the same each time. When every boundary follows the pattern, the phrase is heard as a smooth chain.
quests.phoneticRule: When every boundary in a chunk is a consonant + vowel boundary, all of them can link, producing a continuous chain.
